You are working with your brain instead of against it. Using a tool well is planning, not dependence.

When is the best time to do chores if you take ADHD medication?

During the stretch of your day when starting things feels lightest. If your routine is steady, that stretch tends to show up around the same time each day, and two or three days of casual noticing will find it. Put your five-minute reset inside that slot and guard it from the phone. Any questions about the medication itself belong with your prescriber.

What should I do on days when the window never shows up?

Fall back to something smaller and kinder. Pick one tiny anchor, like clearing the mug next to you or starting the dishwasher, and let that count as the reset for the day. A no-window day is information about your day, not a verdict on you. A system that can shrink is a system you will still be using next month.

Sources:
- Cortese S, Adamo N, Del Giovane C, et al. (2018). Comparative efficacy and tolerability of medications for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in children, adolescents, and adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. The Lancet Psychiatry, 5(9), 727-738. https://doi.org/10.1016/S2215-0366(18)30269-4
- Volkow ND, Wang GJ, Kollins SH, et al. (2009). Evaluating dopamine reward pathway in ADHD: clinical implications. JAMA, 302(10), 1084-1091. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2009.1308


## The ADHD bathroom reset that actually gets done
URL: https://neurotidy.co/articles/adhd-bathroom-reset.html
Published: 2026-08-30 · Updated: 2026-08-30
Author: Mara Ellery (pen name of the founder)

An ADHD bathroom reset that actually gets done is a five-minute wipe-and-go in a fixed order, done right after a shower you were taking anyway: counter clear, sink and taps, mirror, toilet, floor spot-check, out. It works because it removes every decision and every separate start, and it replaces the deep clean you keep postponing.

Why the smallest room is the hardest one

The bathroom should be the easy win. It is tiny, there is almost nothing to put away, and yet it is the room most people with ADHD admit they avoid. The reason is that a bathroom is not one job. It is the sink, the taps, the mirror, the toilet, the floor, the shower, the bin. Six or seven small tasks, each with its own start, wearing a trench coat and calling itself "clean the bathroom".

Starting is the expensive part. Task initiation and planning are among the executive functions most reliably impaired in ADHD (Willcutt et al., 2005), so a room that demands six separate starts is six chances to stall. You stand in the doorway, your brain quietly asks "which one first", and the answer never comes.

Why it feels like an hour and takes five minutes

Ask someone with ADHD how long it takes to clean a bathroom and they will say forty minutes, an hour, "the whole evening". Time it once and the honest number for a reset is four to six minutes. That gap is not laziness or exaggeration. Time perception runs differently in ADHD, and dull tasks in particular get sized up as far longer than they are (Ptacek et al., 2019).

A task your brain has filed as an hour long gets pushed to "later", and later needs a free hour, which never arrives. This is the same loop that keeps the dreaded-task list untouched for weeks. The fix is not motivation. It is a timer and a number you have measured yourself.

The reframe: a reset, not a clean

You are never going to deep clean the bathroom on a Tuesday, and you do not need to. What you need is a bathroom that reads as clean to you and to anyone who walks in, twice a week, forever. That is a reset: surfaces you see, in a fixed order, timer on, stop when it rings. Grout is a different project for a different day, and honestly it may never be that day, and the bathroom is still fine.

Weak internal self-regulation is the core of the most-cited model of ADHD, and the recommended answer in that model is to move the control outside your head into cues and fixed sequences (Barkley, 1997). So the reset is glued to a shower. You are already in the room, already warm, already past the hardest start. The reset is what happens on the way out, the same way the closing-shift reset is glued to the end of dinner.

The fixed order, and why the order matters

The order goes top to bottom and clean to dirty: counter, sink and taps, mirror, toilet, floor. Top to bottom so anything you knock down gets caught by the floor step. Clean to dirty so one cloth does the whole room and the toilet is last. Fixing the order means you never decide what is next; the previous step decides for you.

Keep one cloth, one spray, and a small bin bag under the sink so the reset starts without a trip to another room. A trip is a fresh start, and fresh starts are where ADHD resets die. The shower card in the free ADHD task cards uses the same idea for the shower itself: two alarms and a fixed wash order, so the reset that follows has a reliable trigger.

The fix: the five-minute bathroom reset

Right after your shower, set a five-minute timer. Wet room, warm you, no decisions. This is the only time the reset happens.

Clear the counter. Everything that lives elsewhere goes in one pile outside the door. Do not sort it now.

Spray and wipe the sink, taps, and mirror with one cloth, in that order. A shiny tap does most of the visual work.

Toilet: seat, rim, and outside with the same cloth, then the cloth goes in the wash. Quick brush of the bowl if it needs it.

Floor spot-check: hair by the sink, the bath mat straightened, bin bag tied if full. Timer rings, you are done, even if something got missed.

FAQ

How often should I clean the bathroom with ADHD?

Do the five-minute reset twice a week, tied to a shower you already take, and stop planning a deep clean at all. Two short resets keep a bathroom presentable indefinitely. If it has been a while, the first reset just takes ten minutes instead of five, and then you are back on the twice-a-week rhythm.

Why is cleaning the bathroom so hard when it's such a small room?

Because a bathroom is a small room with a lot of separate surfaces, and each surface is its own start. Sink, taps, mirror, toilet, floor, shower: that is six tasks pretending to be one, and starting tasks is the part ADHD makes expensive. A fixed order removes the starting problem by making each step the automatic next move.

What is the fastest way to make a bathroom look clean?

Clear the counter and wipe the sink and taps. A clear counter and a shiny tap read as clean to anyone walking in, even if the shower has not been touched. If you have ninety seconds, do those two and nothing else.

Sources:
- Willcutt EG, Doyle AE, Nigg JT, Faraone SV, Pennington BF (2005). Validity of the executive function theory of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analytic review. Biological Psychiatry, 57(11), 1336-1346. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biopsych.2005.02.006
- Ptacek R, Weissenberger S, Braaten E, et al. (2019). Clinical implications of the perception of time in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): a review. Medical Science Monitor, 25, 3918-3924. https://doi.org/10.12659/MSM.914225
- Barkley RA (1997). Behavioral inhibition, sustained attention, and executive functions: constructing a unifying theory of ADHD. Psychological Bulletin, 121(1), 65-94. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.121.1.65


## An ADHD cleaning schedule that actually sticks
URL: https://neurotidy.co/articles/adhd-cleaning-schedule-that-sticks.html
Published: 2026-08-30 · Updated: 2026-08-30
Author: Mara Ellery (pen name of the founder)

An ADHD cleaning schedule that actually sticks has three parts: a short daily reset that is anchored to something you already do, one small weekly task per day from a fixed list, and a bad-day version written underneath every line. It works because it never asks you to feel like cleaning, it only asks you to follow the anchor.

The chart you made in January

You know the one. Colour coded, one row per room, maybe laminated. Monday bathroom, Tuesday floors, Wednesday laundry. It lasted nine days, one bad Tuesday happened, and by Thursday it was a small monument to failure on the fridge. The next chart was more detailed, because clearly the problem was not enough structure.

The problem was never the structure. The chart assumed two things your brain does not reliably supply: that you will feel like doing a boring task at the scheduled time, and that "Tuesday" will feel like Tuesday when it arrives. Neither is safe to assume with ADHD, and a schedule built on unsafe assumptions falls over the first time they are wrong.

Motivation is not a reliable engine

Most schedules quietly run on motivation. But a boring task with a payoff that is hours away is exactly the kind of task an ADHD brain tends to lose to anything more immediately rewarding; researchers describe this as delay aversion, a strong pull away from waiting for a reward (Sonuga-Barke, 2003). Imaging work in adults with ADHD also points to differences in the dopamine reward pathway that shape motivation itself (Volkow et al., 2009).

So the fix is not to try harder to want it. The fix is to build a schedule that runs even when you do not. That means anchors instead of feelings, and timers instead of clock times.

Anchors beat clock times

"Clean the kitchen at 8pm" needs you to notice that it is 8pm, remember the plan, and feel ready. Time perception itself is different in ADHD, which is why 8pm so often arrives at 9:40 (Ptacek et al., 2019). "Wipe the counter while the kettle boils" needs none of that. The kettle is the reminder, the plan, and the timer in one object.

An anchor is anything you already do daily without deciding to: the kettle, the shower, feeding the cat, the end of the evening show, taking your meds. Attach one tiny cleaning action to each anchor and the schedule starts running on things that already happen. If you take medication, the meds window is the best anchor of all for the reset that needs the most starting power.

The bad-day line is what keeps it alive

Every schedule that ever died on you died on a bad day. Skipping one day broke the streak, a broken streak felt like a failed system, and the all-or-nothing switch flipped to nothing.

So every line on your schedule gets a second, smaller line underneath: the version you do on a bad day. Under "closing shift, 15 minutes" goes "rinse one mug, tie the bin bag." Under "one load of laundry" goes "clothes into the basket." On a bad day you do the small line, and the day still counts. The bare-minimum day is the full version of that idea, and it is worth reading before you write your own lines.

The fix: build the schedule in ten minutes

List your anchors. Write down five things you already do every day without deciding: kettle, shower, meds, dinner, the show. These are the only "times" your schedule uses.

Attach one tiny action to each anchor. Kettle: wipe the counter. Shower: spray the tiles while the water warms up. Dinner: run the dishwasher. The show: the 5-minute closing shift. Each one must fit inside the anchor, not after it.

Pick one weekly task per weekday from a short fixed list, and write it on a single sticky note: Monday bathroom sink, Tuesday one load of laundry, Wednesday floor of one room, Thursday fridge shelf, Friday bins and recycling. If you miss a day, you skip it, you do not catch up.

Write the bad-day line under every item, smaller and easier by a lot. That line is not a consolation prize; on a bad day it is the entire job and it counts.

Set a timer every single time. Five to fifteen minutes, then stop. Put the sticky note where the first anchor happens, usually next to the kettle, and put a card from the free printable task cards where the hardest task happens. After two weeks, cut anything you skipped more than twice.

FAQ

What does a realistic ADHD cleaning schedule look like?

One short daily reset of five to fifteen minutes, anchored to something you already do like the kettle or the evening show, plus one weekly task per day picked from a short list. No colour-coded chart. If it does not fit on a sticky note, it is too big to survive a bad week.

How do I stick to a cleaning routine with ADHD when I lose motivation?

Stop relying on motivation and rely on anchors instead. Attach the reset to an existing habit, keep a timer running, and write the bad-day version underneath so a low day still counts as done. The routine survives because it never depends on how you feel.

Should I clean every day with ADHD or do one big clean?

Every day, but tiny. A five-minute daily reset keeps the house at a livable baseline, and it removes the dread that makes the big clean impossible to start. The big clean can still happen occasionally, but it stops being the only way the house ever gets clean.

Sources:
- Sonuga-Barke EJS (2003). The dual pathway model of AD/HD: an elaboration of neuro-developmental characteristics. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 27(7), 593-604. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neubiorev.2003.08.005
- Volkow ND, Wang GJ, Kollins SH, et al. (2009). Evaluating dopamine reward pathway in ADHD: clinical implications. JAMA, 302(10), 1084-1091. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2009.1308
- Ptacek R, Weissenberger S, Braaten E, et al. (2019). Clinical implications of the perception of time in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): a review. Medical Science Monitor, 25, 3918-3924. https://doi.org/10.12659/MSM.914225


## ADHD object permanence: why out of sight is out of mind
URL: https://neurotidy.co/articles/adhd-object-permanence-cleaning.html
Published: 2026-08-30 · Updated: 2026-08-30
Author: Mara Ellery (pen name of the founder)

When people with ADHD say they have no object permanence, they mean that anything out of sight drops out of mind: the leftovers behind the milk, the charger in the drawer, the bill in the folder. The research does not call it object permanence, it calls it working memory, and the practical fix is the same either way: store things so your eyes can do the remembering.

The name is wrong, the experience is not

Object permanence, in the textbook sense, is what a baby learns in the first year: the ball still exists behind the cushion. Adults with ADHD have that, so a psychologist hearing "ADHD object permanence" is technically right to wince.

But the people using the phrase are describing something real, they just borrowed the nearest label. Put the yoghurt at the back of the fridge and you no longer own yoghurt. Put the passport somewhere safe and lose it for a year. That is not carelessness. It is what happens when the mental list is short and the visual cue was holding most of it.

What the research actually says

The mechanism has a name: working memory, the small, temporary store that holds information in place while you use it. A meta-analysis of 38 studies found that adults with ADHD show consistent working memory deficits compared with adults without it (Alderson et al., 2013). A larger review across 83 studies found working memory to be one of the executive functions most reliably affected in ADHD (Willcutt et al., 2005).

Working memory is what lets you keep "the yoghurt is behind the milk" alive in your head while you are doing something else. Barkley's account of ADHD places it among the core functions involved in holding goals and information in mind across time (Barkley, 1997). When that store is smaller or leakier, your environment has to carry the difference. A visible object is a reminder you do not have to hold. A hidden one is a reminder you have to generate yourself, which is the harder part.

So the honest version is: with ADHD, out of sight really is out of mind, because sight was doing the remembering. Said that way, the fix is obvious, and it is not "try harder."

Why this makes your home look messy

Here is the trap. You know that things you put away disappear, so you leave them out. The charger stays on the desk, the vitamins on the counter, the mail on the chair. Each one is a sensible workaround. Together they look like clutter, and someone tells you to just put things away.

The cup in every room is the same story: each cup was put down where it was in use, and then it stopped existing. The floordrobe is the same story with clothes. The room in why is my room always messy relapses for the same reason. You are not failing to put things away; you are choosing visible over lost.

The reframe: make visible the system, not the accident

Leaving things out on purpose, in a designed spot, is not mess. It is storage that fits your brain. A tray for the charger and keys is visible storage; the charger loose among the mail is a pile. Same object, different system.

Once storage has to be see-through, most organising advice inverts. Drawers lose to open bins, cupboards to shelves, opaque baskets to clear ones. You are not decorating, you are building an external memory.

The fix: storage your eyes can read

Give every daily-use item exactly one visible home. Keys and charger in one tray by the door, meds on a small dish by the kettle, glasses on the nightstand. If it has two homes it has none.

Swap closed for open where things keep getting lost. Clear bins instead of drawers for cables and toiletries, an open shelf for the things you cook with daily, hooks for the three jackets you actually wear.

Move the fridge to the front. Eye level, front row, is the only shelf that exists. Leftovers and anything with a short life go there, in clear containers.

Cut the object count. Every extra thing is one more item for the system to display. Fewer mugs, fewer half-used bottles, fewer maybe-clothes. Less to read, less to reset.

Label anything that must stay closed. If a drawer has to be a drawer, put a label on the front that lists what is inside, so the drawer itself becomes the reminder. Then stick one of the free printable task cards where the mess usually lands, because a card in sight is a plan you do not have to remember.

FAQ

Is object permanence a real ADHD symptom?

Not in the textbook sense. Object permanence is a developmental milestone that adults with ADHD have. What the community calls ADHD object permanence is a working memory difference: when a thing leaves your sight, it also drops out of the mental list you were holding. The label is loose, the experience is real, and the research on working memory backs it up.

Why do I forget things exist when I put them away?

Because putting something in a drawer removes the visual cue that was doing the remembering for you. With weaker working memory the cue was carrying most of the load, so once it is gone the item is effectively gone too. Visible storage keeps the cue in place, which is why open shelves and clear bins work where drawers fail.

How do I organise my home if I forget what I own?

Store things where you use them, in containers you can see into, and keep one visible home per daily item. Fewer objects helps more than better drawers. The goal is not a tidy-looking room, it is a room where your eyes do the remembering.

Sources:
- Alderson RM, Kasper LJ, Hudec KL, Patros CHG (2013). Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and working memory in adults: a meta-analytic review. Neuropsychology, 27(3), 287-302. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032371
- Willcutt EG, Doyle AE, Nigg JT, Faraone SV, Pennington BF (2005). Validity of the executive function theory of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analytic review. Biological Psychiatry, 57(11), 1336-1346. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biopsych.2005.02.006
- Barkley RA (1997). Behavioral inhibition, sustained attention, and executive functions: constructing a unifying theory of ADHD. Psychological Bulletin, 121(1), 65-94. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.121.1.65


## The bare-minimum ADHD cleaning day (for when it's all too much)
URL: https://neurotidy.co/articles/bare-minimum-cleaning-day.html
Published: 2026-08-30 · Updated: 2026-08-30
Author: Mara Ellery (pen name of the founder)

A bare-minimum ADHD cleaning day is three short anchors attached to things you already do: a two-minute kitchen close after your last meal, a one-minute bathroom wipe after brushing your teeth, and a three-minute bedroom path clear before bed. Under ten minutes, no deciding, and the house holds steady until you have capacity again.

What "too much" actually means for an ADHD brain

There are weeks when the house is not the problem. Work is on fire, or someone is sick, or you are two weeks into a low patch and the dishes have become a shape you walk past. Cleaning advice written for normal weeks does not survive these ones. You need a version of the house that runs on almost nothing.

ADHD is, in one of the most-cited models, a difference in self-regulation: the internal signals that would normally start and steer a boring task are weaker, so external structure has to do that job instead (Barkley, 1997). During a hard stretch you have even less internal signal than usual. The trick is not more willpower. It is more scaffolding, and less of it to hold.

Why "a little every day" quietly fails

The standard rescue plan is to do a little every day. It sounds gentle. In practice it hands your brain a fresh decision each evening: what counts as a little, and where. Planning and sticking with dull tasks are two of the executive functions most consistently reduced in ADHD (Willcutt et al., 2005), so the plan collapses at exactly the point where you have to invent it.

Maintenance cleaning also has the worst payoff of any chore. Nothing looks different after you wipe a counter that was mostly fine. Reduced reward signalling in adult ADHD is well documented (Volkow et al., 2009), and it means the tasks with no visible result are the ones that vanish first when you are stretched. You are not being careless. The task is invisible to the part of your brain that starts things.

The reframe: anchors, not a routine

A routine is a list you have to remember and start. An anchor is a tiny task glued to something you already do without thinking. You already eat a last meal. You already brush your teeth. You already walk to bed. Each of those moments gets one short action attached to it, so the action starts because the habit before it started.

The three anchors are deliberately in three different rooms, so the whole house gets a touch every day without you ever cleaning the whole house. They are also short enough that the finish line is visible before you begin, which matters far more than how much you get done. If even the anchors are out of reach some days, the low-energy list is the version for that.

What a bare-minimum house looks like, honestly

It is not clean. Laundry is in a pile. The floor could use a hoover. There may be a doom pile on the table. What it is not is worse than yesterday. The sink is usable, the toilet is fine, you can walk to the bed. That is the entire goal of a hard stretch: hold the line, do not lose ground, and let the recovery happen later with the 15-minute closing shift when you have the capacity for it.

Write the three anchors on a card and stick it on the fridge, or print the bad-day card from the free ADHD task cards. The point of the card is that on a bad day you read instead of deciding.

The fix: the three-anchor day

After your last meal: two-minute kitchen close. Food back in the fridge, dishes into hot soapy water, one wipe of the counter you cook on. Timer on, stop when it rings.

After brushing your teeth: one-minute bathroom wipe. One cloth over the sink and taps, towel back on the hook, done. Do not touch the shower.

Before bed: three-minute path clear. Move whatever is on the floor between the door and the bed to the sides. Do not sort, do not fold, just clear the path.

Tape the three anchors where each one happens: by the sink, on the mirror, by the bedroom door. Reading beats remembering.

When the hard stretch ends, do one 15-minute closing-shift reset instead of a deep clean. The anchors kept the house recoverable, so recovery is small.

FAQ

What is the bare minimum I should clean each day with ADHD?

Three anchor moments: a two-minute kitchen close after your last meal, a one-minute bathroom wipe after you brush your teeth, and a three-minute bedroom path clear before bed. That is under ten minutes and it keeps the house livable. Nothing else is required on a bare-minimum day.

How long can I run on bare minimum before it becomes a problem?

Indefinitely, if the three anchors actually happen. A house on bare minimum is not clean but it is not getting worse, and that is the whole job during a hard stretch. When the stretch ends, one 15-minute reset brings it back. You do not need a deep clean to recover.

Why can't I just do a little bit of everything?

Because a little bit of everything means deciding what a little bit is, in every room, every day. Decisions are the expensive part for an ADHD brain, especially during a bad stretch. Fixed anchors attached to things you already do remove the deciding, which is why they survive weeks that free-form tidying does not.

Sources:
- Barkley RA (1997). Behavioral inhibition, sustained attention, and executive functions: constructing a unifying theory of ADHD. Psychological Bulletin, 121(1), 65-94. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.121.1.65
- Willcutt EG, Doyle AE, Nigg JT, Faraone SV, Pennington BF (2005). Validity of the executive function theory of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analytic review. Biological Psychiatry, 57(11), 1336-1346. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biopsych.2005.02.006
- Volkow ND, Wang GJ, Kollins SH, et al. (2009). Evaluating dopamine reward pathway in ADHD: clinical implications. JAMA, 302(10), 1084-1091. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2009.1308


## How to declutter a doom pile step by step (ADHD method)
URL: https://neurotidy.co/articles/declutter-doom-pile-step-by-step.html
Published: 2026-08-30 · Updated: 2026-08-30
Author: Mara Ellery (pen name of the founder)

To declutter a doom pile with ADHD, pick one pile, set a 10-minute timer, and sort every object into four boxes by address, not by verdict: trash, belongs elsewhere, needs a decision, stays here. You do not decide what to keep today, you only decide where each thing goes next, and you stop when the timer rings.

Why the pile beat you last time

A doom pile is not junk. It is a stack of small decisions you did not have the fuel to make at the time, so you moved the object somewhere flat and promised yourself later. Each object is a tiny "what do I do with this," and the pile is forty of them stacked on a chair.

The usual advice is to go through it. That means holding forty open questions in your head at once and answering them in order. Working memory, the part of your brain that holds things in place while you work on them, is measurably weaker in adults with ADHD (Alderson et al., 2013). So you pick up the receipt, wonder if you need it, put it down, pick up the charger, and twenty minutes later the pile has been rearranged, not cleared. That is the wrong tool for the job, not a willpower failure.

Sorting is not deciding

Here is the reframe that makes the pile move. There are two separate jobs hiding inside "clear the pile": sorting things by where they go, and deciding what happens to the hard ones. Most people try to do both at once, and the hard ones jam the whole line.

Sorting is mechanical. Trash is trash, a mug belongs in the kitchen. Deciding is expensive. Do I keep the receipt? Is this cable dead? Planning and organising multi-step work is exactly the executive function skill that a large body of research finds impaired in ADHD (Willcutt et al., 2005). So you take the deciding out of the session entirely. Anything that needs a real decision goes in a box labelled exactly that, and the box is allowed to sit there.

If the pile is mostly clothes, the same logic applies with one basket instead of four boxes, and the clothes chair guide has that version. If you are not sure whether what you have is a doom pile or something heavier, doom piles vs hoarding draws the line kindly, because hoarding symptoms do show up more often alongside ADHD (Morein-Zamir et al., 2022) and deserve a different kind of help than a timer.

Why the timer matters more than the boxes

A doom pile has no natural end. You can always sort one more thing, so your brain reads the whole task as infinite and refuses to start. A 10-minute timer gives it an end it can see. You are doing ten minutes of sorting, and ten minutes is a size you can begin.

The timer also protects you from the four-hour spiral that ends at 1am with the pile half on the floor. When the timer rings, you stop. What is sorted stays sorted. What is not sorted waits for the next ten minutes, and the next ten minutes is easier because the pile is smaller.

The fix: the four-box sort

Pick one pile. Not the room, not the surface, one pile. Put something on to listen to, then set a timer for 10 minutes. Starting the timer is the whole commitment.

Set up four containers where the pile is. A bin bag for trash, a laundry basket or box for belongs elsewhere, a shoebox for needs a decision, and the cleared surface itself for stays here.

Take the top object and put it in a box by address, not by verdict. Mail you might need goes in decisions. A cup goes in elsewhere. Packaging goes in trash. If you hold something longer than a breath, it is a decision, so it goes in that box.

When the timer rings, stop. Take the bin bag out. Walk the elsewhere basket around the house once, dropping things at their homes without tidying those homes.

Put the decision box somewhere visible and book it a body double: a friend on speaker, a video call, a cleaning stream. Ten minutes with company clears a decision box that has sat alone for a month. If a category keeps coming back, give it a tray or open basket where it lands, so the next pile has somewhere to go instead of the chair. The free printable task cards have this exact sort as a card you can stick next to the pile.

FAQ

How long does it take to clear a doom pile with ADHD?

One pile, one 10-minute timer, and you stop when it rings even if the pile is not finished. Most piles need two or three of those sessions, not one heroic afternoon. The short timer is the point: a session you can actually start beats a session you keep avoiding.

What are the four boxes for a doom pile?

Trash, belongs elsewhere, needs a decision, and stays here. Every object gets an address, not a verdict. The decision box is allowed to exist; it holds the hard things so they stop blocking the easy ones.

Why does my doom pile keep coming back after I clear it?

Because the pile is where things land when they have no home you can see. If the same category keeps piling up, that category needs a visible spot, like a tray or an open basket, near where it lands. Clear the pile, then give the repeat offenders a landing place, and the pile shrinks instead of rebuilding.

Sources:
- Alderson RM, Kasper LJ, Hudec KL, Patros CHG (2013). Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and working memory in adults: a meta-analytic review. Neuropsychology, 27(3), 287-302. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032371
- Willcutt EG, Doyle AE, Nigg JT, Faraone SV, Pennington BF (2005). Validity of the executive function theory of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analytic review. Biological Psychiatry, 57(11), 1336-1346. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biopsych.2005.02.006
- Morein-Zamir S, Kasese M, Chamberlain SR, Trachtenberg E (2022). Elevated levels of hoarding in ADHD: a special link with inattention. Journal of Psychiatric Research, 145, 167-174. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpsychires.2021.12.024


## The low-energy ADHD cleaning list for bad brain days
URL: https://neurotidy.co/articles/low-energy-adhd-cleaning-list.html
Published: 2026-08-30 · Updated: 2026-08-30
Author: Mara Ellery (pen name of the founder)

A low-energy ADHD cleaning list is six tiny tasks that keep tomorrow from being worse: rinse one mug, tie the trash, put dishes in water, clear the path to the bed, one glass of water, outfit on the chair. It takes under ten minutes, needs zero decisions, and on a bad brain day it counts as a full win.

Why a bad brain day is a capacity problem, not a laziness problem

Some days you wake up and the kitchen looks the same as yesterday but feels three times heavier. Nothing changed in the room. What changed is how much your brain can hold. On those days the systems that start tasks and keep them going are running on almost nothing.

That is not a mood you can talk yourself out of. Starting a task, planning its steps, and staying with something boring are all executive functions, and those are exactly the functions that test as impaired in ADHD across dozens of studies (Willcutt et al., 2005). On a good day you compensate. On a bad day the compensation is gone, and "just do a quick tidy" turns into staring at the sink for twenty minutes.

Why "do what you can" makes bad days worse

The advice you usually get is gentle and useless: do what you can, be kind to yourself, rest. The problem is that "what you can" is an open question, and open questions are the thing your brain cannot answer today. So you either do nothing, or you start something big, run out halfway, and now the room is worse and so are you.

Working memory is the part of the brain that holds a plan while you carry it out, and it is one of the most consistently reduced abilities in adults with ADHD (Alderson et al., 2013). On a bad day it is smaller still. A list you have to invent on the spot lives in working memory. A list taped to the fridge does not.

The reframe: a floor, not a goal

Stop asking what you should clean today. Decide, once, on a normal day, what the floor is: the smallest set of actions that stops the house from sliding into unbearable. Then on bad days you do not make a plan, you run the floor. Hitting the floor is a ten out of ten. There is no extra credit and no failing grade.

Boring tasks with no payoff are the first to drop when reward processing runs differently, which is well described in ADHD (Sonuga-Barke, 2003). The floor works with that instead of against it. Every item is short enough that the finish line is visible before you start, and finishing is the only reward the task needs.

If bad days are stacking up, the bare-minimum cleaning day is the same idea stretched over a whole day, and the meds window can tell you when your brain is most likely to show up.

What is on the list, and why each item earns its place

Every item exists to protect tomorrow-you. A rinsed mug means coffee happens. Tied trash means no smell and no fruit flies. Dishes in water means they will not fossilise. A clear path means you will not step on a charger at 2am. A glass of water and an outfit on the chair mean the morning starts without a decision. Nothing on the list is about how the house looks. It is about removing the things that make the next bad day harder.

The list lives on a card by the sink, and the same card is in the free ADHD task cards as the Bad-Day Floor, so you can print it instead of remembering it.

The fix: the six-item bad-day floor

Rinse one mug and put it by the kettle. Just one. That is tomorrow's coffee handled.

Tie the kitchen trash bag. You do not have to take it out. Tied is enough to stop the smell.

Put the dishes in hot soapy water and walk away. Soaking counts as progress and makes the real wash half the job.

Clear the walking path from the bed to the bathroom. Kick things to the side, do not sort them.

Fill a glass of water for the nightstand and put tomorrow's outfit on the chair. Zero morning decisions.

That is five actions and about eight minutes. If you did them, the day counts. If you did two of them, the day still counts, and the other three are waiting for tomorrow without judgement.

FAQ

What should I clean when I have no energy and ADHD?

Only the things that make tomorrow worse if you skip them: one mug rinsed, trash tied, dishes soaking, the path to the bed clear. That is the whole list. Everything else can wait for a day when your brain shows up, and skipping it today costs you nothing.

Is it okay to do the bare minimum on bad days?

It is the correct move, not a failure. A bad brain day is a capacity problem, not a motivation problem, and pushing through it usually ends in a half-finished mess and a worse mood. A tiny fixed list keeps the house from sliding into unbearable while your energy comes back.

How do I stop bad days from turning into a week of mess?

Make the bad-day list boring and fixed so it runs on autopilot. Same six items, same order, no deciding. When it is written down and taped somewhere visible, your brain does not have to hold it, and a bad day stays a bad day instead of becoming a bad month.

Sources:
- Willcutt EG, Doyle AE, Nigg JT, Faraone SV, Pennington BF (2005). Validity of the executive function theory of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analytic review. Biological Psychiatry, 57(11), 1336-1346. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biopsych.2005.02.006
- Alderson RM, Kasper LJ, Hudec KL, Patros CHG (2013). Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and working memory in adults: a meta-analytic review. Neuropsychology, 27(3), 287-302. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032371
- Sonuga-Barke EJS (2003). The dual pathway model of AD/HD: an elaboration of neuro-developmental characteristics. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 27(7), 593-604. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neubiorev.2003.08.005


## What is the 1-3-5 rule for ADHD, and does it work for cleaning?
URL: https://neurotidy.co/articles/1-3-5-rule-adhd.html
Published: 2026-09-03 · Updated: 2026-09-03
Author: Mara Ellery (pen name of the founder)

The 1-3-5 rule for ADHD is a daily list with a fixed shape: one big task, three medium tasks, five small tasks, and nothing else. Nine things, sized the night before, so the day starts with the sorting already done. It was not invented for ADHD, but a capped list happens to fit the exact place an ADHD brain stalls: staring at twenty equally loud items and choosing none.

Where the rule comes from

The 1-3-5 rule (you will also see it written 1/3/5) comes from a 2013 article by Alex Cavoulacos, co-founder of The Muse, later reprinted by Fast Company. Her premise was about office work: on any given day you can realistically finish one big thing, three medium things, and five small things, so write the list in that shape and stop pretending the other thirty items are happening today.

It has since been picked up by ADHD coaches and forums as a planning method, mostly by word of mouth. To be plain about it: there is no study of the 1-3-5 rule in people with ADHD. What is studied is the problem it sidesteps, and that is why it is worth your attention.

Why a capped list suits an ADHD brain

An open-ended to-do list asks you to hold every item in mind, rank them, and pick one, all before doing anything. Working memory is one of the most consistently reduced functions in adult ADHD (Alderson et al., 2013), so that first step, holding the list, is already the expensive part. Twenty items do not get ranked. They get looked at, and then the phone comes out.

The 1-3-5 rule moves the sorting to a different moment. You size the tasks the night before, when nothing is being asked of you, and the morning list is nine items with their size already decided. That is the pattern the standard model of ADHD recommends in general: when internal regulation is weak, put the structure outside your head (Barkley, 1997). The rule is a small piece of external structure that costs one minute to set up.

The five small tasks do a second job. ADHD involves a weaker response to reward, particularly delayed reward (Volkow et al., 2009), which is why "clean the house" produces nothing and "put the cups in the sink" sometimes does. Five small, visible completions before lunch are five real signals that something happened today. It is the same reason the low-energy list is built from tiny steps.

How to size cleaning tasks (this is where it goes wrong)

People with ADHD reliably misjudge how long dull tasks take, in both directions (Ptacek et al., 2019). A bathroom reset feels like an hour and takes five minutes. Sorting one doom pile feels like ten minutes and takes forty. If you size by feel, the big slot fills with something small and the small slots fill with things that are secretly big, and the rule collapses on day two.

So size by measured minutes and by the number of separate starts a job needs:

Big (one per day): 20 to 45 minutes, one zone. The kitchen closing reset. One doom pile sorted to empty. A laundry cycle carried all the way from basket to drawer. Anything with more than one zone is two big tasks, so it is tomorrow's.

Medium (three): 5 to 15 minutes, one surface or one load. Dishes. The coffee table cleared. One bin round through every room. The chair.

Small (five): under 5 minutes, one object or one motion. Cups walk. Wipe the bathroom counter. Bag of rubbish out. Pillows back on the sofa. Bins out to the kerb.

Time each one once with a real timer and write the number down. After a week you will have a private table of what things actually cost, and the sizing stops being guesswork.

What a 1-3-5 cleaning day looks like

A Tuesday, nothing special, house in its normal state:

1 big: kitchen reset after dinner, timer at 25 minutes. Counters, sink, dishwasher on, floor spot-check. Stop when it rings.

3 medium: one load of laundry to the dryer; coffee table and floor around it cleared; bathroom five-minute reset after the shower.

5 small: cups walk through every room; bag of post sorted into keep and bin; bins out; sofa cushions back; one chair cleared of clothes.

That is the whole day. It looks thin on paper, and that is the point. A list that fits in one glance is a list you can start. The fuller version you would have written, the one with "deep clean the fridge" and "sort the garage" on it, is the list you have been not starting for three months.

The rules inside the rule

Three things keep it from turning back into the old list. First, nothing gets added mid-day. A new task goes on tomorrow's sheet, not today's. Second, an unfinished big task is not a failure, it is tomorrow's big task, and you do not double up to compensate. Third, on a day when you cannot function, the five small ones are the entire plan and the other slots stay empty. The rule has not failed on that day. It has stopped you writing down a day you could not have, which is the whole job of a cap.

If even five small tasks is too much, use the bare-minimum day instead and come back to 1-3-5 tomorrow.

The fix: set up your first 1-3-5 list tonight

Tonight, not tomorrow morning, write nine lines on paper or a note: one big, three medium, five small. Paper is better; it does not have a feed.

Pick the big one from the zone that bothers you most when you walk in. Set its timer length now, 20 to 45 minutes.

Fill the three medium slots with one-surface or one-load jobs. If a job needs more than one start, it is big, not medium.

Fill the five small slots with under-five-minute single motions. The free task cards are already sized this way if you want to pull from them.

In the morning, start with a small one, never the big one. The first completion is what unlocks the rest, and a big task is the worst possible first start.

FAQ

Does the 1-3-5 rule actually work for ADHD?

There is no clinical trial of the 1-3-5 rule itself. What is well studied is the problem it works around: a long, unsorted list overloads working memory and stalls task initiation, and a short list with the size decided in advance removes both. So it works for the same reason a timer works. It is a container, not a treatment, and on a bad day even the five small ones count.

What counts as a big, medium, or small task when cleaning?

Size by time and by how many separate starts it needs, not by how important it feels. Big is 20 to 45 minutes and one zone: the kitchen reset, one doom pile sorted, the laundry cycle from basket to drawer. Medium is 5 to 15 minutes and one surface or one load: dishes, the coffee table, one bin bag round. Small is under 5 minutes and one object: cups walk, chair cleared, bathroom counter wiped.

What if I only manage the five small tasks?

Then you did the five small tasks, and the house is better than it was. The rule caps the day; it does not require the day to be full. Move the big one to tomorrow's slot and do not add anything to make up for it. On a low-energy day the small five alone are the whole plan.

Is the 1-3-5 rule the same as the 1/3/5 rule?

Yes. Same method, written with slashes or dashes depending on who is typing it. It comes from a 2013 productivity article by Alex Cavoulacos and was not designed for ADHD; it has been adopted because a fixed-size list happens to suit how an ADHD brain handles lists.

Sources:
- Alderson RM, Kasper LJ, Hudec KL, Patros CHG (2013). Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and working memory in adults: a meta-analytic review. Neuropsychology, 27(3), 287-302. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032371
- Barkley RA (1997). Behavioral inhibition, sustained attention, and executive functions: constructing a unifying theory of ADHD. Psychological Bulletin, 121(1), 65-94. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.121.1.65
- Volkow ND, Wang GJ, Kollins SH, et al. (2009). Evaluating dopamine reward pathway in ADHD: clinical implications. JAMA, 302(10), 1084-1091. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2009.1308
- Ptacek R, Weissenberger S, Braaten E, et al. (2019). Clinical implications of the perception of time in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): a review. Medical Science Monitor, 25, 3918-3924. https://doi.org/10.12659/MSM.914225


## About Neurotidy and who writes the guides
URL: https://neurotidy.co/about/

Neurotidy publishes plain-language cleaning and organizing systems for people with ADHD, built around how the brain actually handles starting, deciding, remembering and time, rather than around willpower or shame. Everything on the site is written under the pen name Mara Ellery by Neurotidy's founder.

Who writes this

Mara Ellery is the pen name of Neurotidy's founder. One person writes every guide, builds every card and answers the messages. The pen name keeps the brand about the systems rather than one face. There are no credentials behind it, and none are claimed.

The guides come from a specific method. We read and sorted more than 21,000 real ADHD threads about cleaning and home life: the chair of clothes, the sink, the doom pile, the shower nobody can start. The patterns that came up again and again became the systems. Then we checked each mechanism we describe (working memory, time perception, reward and motivation, task initiation) against published research, and every guide lists the papers it leans on, with DOIs, at the end.

Neurotidy is not a clinician. Nothing here is medical advice, a diagnosis, or a substitute for talking to a professional about ADHD, medication or your mental health.

What we make

Five free printable ADHD task cards. Direct PDF, no email, every card has a bad-day version.

The ADHD Home Reset. The full 20-card deck plus a short guide, $9.

The Whole Home Reset. 56 cards across every room, plus reset-day and bad-brain-day decks, $27 on Gumroad.

The guides, which are free and always will be.

Editorial rules

No shame language. A pile is a system output, not a character flaw. We name the mechanism, then give the fix.

Every claim about the brain carries a citation. If we say working memory or time perception is involved, the paper is listed at the end of the guide. If we cannot find one, we say the idea is anecdotal.

Dates on everything. Every guide shows when it was published and when it was last reviewed.

We update, and we show it. When a guide changes, the reviewed date changes with it. Old advice does not sit around pretending to be current.

Honest about the products. The free cards are really free. The paid decks are described by what is in them, not by numbers we made up.

## The ADHD Home Reset: 20 printable task cards ($9)
URL: https://neurotidy.co/adhd-home-reset/

The ADHD Home Reset is a $9 deck of 20 printable task cards plus a short guide, built for people whose homes fall apart not from laziness but from how an ADHD brain handles starting, deciding and remembering. Each card lives where its task happens, breaks the job into a few steps, and has a bad-day version at the bottom so there is always a size of the task you can do.

What you get

Twenty task cards and one guide, both as print-ready PDFs. The cards are set up four to an A4 sheet with dashed cut lines. The guide is short on purpose: why routines fail for ADHD brains, the five levers that quietly replace willpower, and six room-by-room playbooks, each with its own bad-day version.

The idea is not a routine you white-knuckle. It is a card you read at the sink, a card on the mirror, a card on the pile. You never have to hold the whole list in your head, because the card is holding it.

Who it is for

Late-diagnosed and self-identified ADHD adults who are tired of being told to just try harder. People whose kitchen swings between spotless and disaster with nothing in between. People who can plan a deep clean but cannot start a five-minute one. If wanting to clean and being able to start feel like two different circuits in your head, this was written for you.

What is in the deck

Kitchen: dishes, counters and the nightly sink reset. The four hidden decisions in every dish get removed, one card at a time.

Laundry: the wash, the folding wall and the clean pile that never gets put away.

Bathroom: the 2-alarm shower and a small reset that keeps the room usable.

Trash: the bag, the bins and the walk to the curb as separate, startable steps.

Doom piles: the full triage card, plus what to do with the decision box afterwards.

Mornings: a launch sequence that does not depend on how you slept.

Evenings: the closing-shift reset as a card, so tomorrow starts already handled.

Every card carries a bad-day line. On hard days that line is the entire job, and doing it counts as a full win. You are never failing the system. The system bends to the day you are having.

## The 4 ADHD mess types (and the first fix for each)
URL: https://neurotidy.co/adhd-mess-types/

ADHD mess almost always takes one of four shapes: the Doom Piler, the Floordrobe Keeper, the Out-of-Sight Out-of-Mind, and the Churn and Burn. Each one comes from a different mechanism, so each one has a different first move, and none of them mean you are lazy.

Why sort mess into types

"Just clean up" fails because it treats every mess the same. A pile of deferred decisions, a floor covered in clothes, a counter full of things left out so they are not forgotten, and a kitchen that swings from spotless to disaster are four different problems. The fix for one makes another worse. Put the Out-of-Sight person's things in drawers and they lose everything. Tell the Churn and Burn person to deep clean and you feed the swing.

This framework is Neurotidy's own, built from the patterns that kept repeating across more than 21,000 real ADHD threads about home life. It is a way to pick the right first card, not a diagnosis. Not sure which one you are? The 60-second quiz asks six questions about your actual home and tells you.

The Doom Piler

Every flat surface holds a someday-pile: mail, a charger, a plate, the thing you will deal with later. You mostly know what is in there. You just cannot make it not exist. The pile is every deferred decision stacked in one place, and the fix is to sort without deciding. Read about the Doom Piler.

The Floordrobe Keeper

Clothes live on the floor, the chair, the exercise bike, and clean and dirty have merged into one layer. Putting clothes away is six invisible steps your brain reads as one wall, so they stay out. The fix is one basket and one rule. Read about the Floordrobe Keeper.

The Out-of-Sight Out-of-Mind

If you cannot see it, it stops existing, so everything stays out and everything is everywhere. Closed drawers are where things go to die. This is working memory, not mess, and the fix is visible storage instead of hidden storage. Read about the Out-of-Sight Out-of-Mind.

The Churn and Burn

You do not clean, you CLEAN: a four-hour deep-clean spree, spotless for two days, then nothing for three weeks until it is unbearable again. All-or-nothing is the default, and the fix is a tiny floor so the spiral never starts. Read about the Churn and Burn.

All four are valid

None of these is a character flaw. Each is a predictable output of how an ADHD brain handles decisions, working memory, reward and time. The guides on this site explain those mechanisms, with the research they rest on, and the free task cards give each type a first move that fits.


## The Churn and Burn: the all-or-nothing ADHD mess type
URL: https://neurotidy.co/adhd-mess-types/churn-and-burn/

The Churn and Burn is the ADHD mess type where you do not clean, you CLEAN: a four-hour deep-clean spree, spotless for two days, then nothing for three weeks until it is unbearable and you do it all again. All-or-nothing is the ADHD default, and the fix is not more discipline but a tiny floor so it never gets back to unbearable in the first place.

How to recognise it

The kitchen is spotless or a full biohazard, no in-between, and right now it is whichever end of the swing you are on. Storage is perfectly organized for about 48 hours after a deep clean, then it slides. You have a system for your keys that works beautifully for the two days right after you reset everything. The chair is empty because you cleared it hard a couple of days ago. Give it a week.

Clothes get folded and put away, then avalanche, then folded again, then avalanche. That is the Churn and Burn, one of the four ADHD mess types.

What is actually going on

An ADHD brain runs on interest, urgency and reward. A four-hour deep clean has all three: the mess got unbearable (urgency), the transformation is dramatic (reward), and it is a novel project rather than a chore (interest). A five-minute daily tidy has none of them. So the brain does the big one and skips the small ones, and the house cycles.

The shame after the crash makes it worse. You proved you can clean, so why can you not keep it clean? Because the state changed and the system did not. Nothing about the daily inputs moved. The closing-shift reset guide and the schedule that sticks guide explain why fixed, tiny routines beat heroic ones, with the research behind it.

The first card to use: The Bad-Day Floor and Reset Day

On a no-meds or low day, the floor is: teeth, water, one mug rinsed, trash tied, outfit on the chair. That is a 10 out of 10 day. It keeps the spiral from ever starting, because the house never reaches the point where only a four-hour spree can fix it.

The floor is deliberately tiny. It has to be reachable on your worst day, or it is not a floor, it is another thing to fail at. On good days you do the floor and then whatever else you like. On bad days the floor is the whole job and it counts.

The Bad-Day Floor card is in the free five, so start there tonight. The full reset-day and bad-brain-day decks, for walking back in gently after a wrecked week, live in the $27 Whole Home Reset. The $9 ADHD Home Reset sits in between with the everyday rooms.

Guides for the Churn and Burn

The 5-minute ADHD cleaning reset. The closing-shift method that replaces the deep clean.

The bare-minimum cleaning day. What counts as enough on a low day.

An ADHD cleaning schedule that sticks. Why fixed and tiny beats big and heroic.

Other types: the Doom Piler, the Floordrobe Keeper, the Out-of-Sight Out-of-Mind. Not sure? Take the 60-second quiz.


## The Doom Piler: the ADHD mess type of deferred decisions
URL: https://neurotidy.co/adhd-mess-types/doom-piler/

The Doom Piler is the ADHD mess type where every flat surface becomes a someday-pile: the chair, the desk, that one corner of the counter. The pile is not junk and it is not laziness, it is a stack of decisions your brain deferred, and the fix is to sort without deciding.

How to recognise it

There is a pile on the chair, and it is not even clothes. Mail, a charger, a plate, a receipt, the thing you meant to return. The kitchen has a permanent corner where paper goes to wait. When you "tidy", the pile moves to a different surface and keeps existing. You know roughly what is in there. You just cannot make it not exist.

If that is your home, you are a Doom Piler. It is the most common of the four ADHD mess types, and the one people feel the most shame about, because the pile is visible proof of every "later" that never came.

What is actually going on

Every object in the pile is a small open question: keep it, bin it, where does it go, who do I need to call about it. ADHD brains find open-ended small decisions expensive, and there is no deadline and no reward attached to answering them. So the item stalls in limbo, on the nearest flat surface, with the other items that stalled before it.

That is why the pile grows and why it feels impossible to start. It is not one task. It is forty tiny verdicts stacked on top of each other, and your brain reads the stack as a wall. The doom pile guide explains the mechanism in more detail, with the research it rests on.

It is not a character flaw. It is a category with nowhere to go.

The first card to use: Doom Pile Triage

Ten minutes, one pile, four boxes: Trash, Belongs elsewhere, Needs a decision, Keep here. You sort mechanically. No verdicts today, only addresses. When the timer ends you are allowed to stop, and the "needs a decision" box waits for a body double or a better day.

The rule that makes it work is sort, do not decide. Deciding is the expensive part. Sorting into boxes is cheap, and once the pile is four boxes it stops being a monument.

This card is in the free five, so you can try it tonight. The bad-day version is to remove exactly three objects. If the free card clicks, the $9 ADHD Home Reset has the full triage card plus the Bad-Day Floor and the rest of the everyday rooms. Start with the free one though. No pressure.

Guides for the Doom Piler

What is a doom pile? The reframe that clears it, five things at a time.

How to declutter a doom pile step by step. The full triage walk-through.

Doom piles vs hoarding. The difference, and why it lifts the shame.

Other types: the Floordrobe Keeper, the Out-of-Sight Out-of-Mind, the Churn and Burn. Not sure? Take the 60-second quiz.


## The Floordrobe Keeper: ADHD clothes-on-the-floor mess type
URL: https://neurotidy.co/adhd-mess-types/floordrobe-keeper/

The Floordrobe Keeper is the ADHD mess type where clothes live on the floor, the chair and the exercise bike, and clean and dirty have merged into one layer. Putting clothes away is about six invisible steps your brain reads as a single wall, so they stay out, and the fix is one basket and one rule.

How to recognise it

The dresser is basically decorative. Yesterday's jeans are on the floor with your keys still in the pocket. The chair holds clothes that are too clean to wash and too worn to put away. When you finally start picking things up, you hit an invisible step three, get overwhelmed, and they go back down.

The kitchen might honestly be fine. It is the bedroom floor that is the crime scene. That is the Floordrobe Keeper, one of the four ADHD mess types.

What is actually going on

"Put the clothes away" sounds like one task. It is not. Pick it up, decide if it is clean, fold it or hang it, find the right drawer, open it, make room, place it, close it. Six or seven steps, each one a small decision, and no reward at the end except a slightly emptier floor.

ADHD brains run low on exactly that kind of multi-step, low-reward work. The steps do not get done because they never got seen as steps. The floor is not a discipline problem. It is what happens when the distance between "worn" and "stored" is too long for the brain to cross on a Tuesday night. The floordrobe guide and the laundry guide explain the mechanism with the research behind it.

The first card to use: The 5-Minute Floordrobe

One basket, one rule: clean goes back, dirty goes in the basket, and that is the whole job. No folding marathon, no sorting by type, no decisions at 11pm. Five minutes with a timer, then you stop.

The trick is that the card removes the steps instead of asking you to push through them. Clean clothes go back on the nearest shelf or hook, not into a folded stack. Dirty clothes go into one basket, not into a sorted system. The floor clears because the job got shorter, not because you got tougher.

This card is not in the free five. It is in the $9 ADHD Home Reset, which has the full laundry set. The free cards are still the right place to start, because the Bad-Day Floor card ("outfit on the chair" counts) is in there and it is the same format. If the format clicks, the laundry cards will too. The $27 Whole Home Reset adds the full bedroom deck on top.

Guides for the Floordrobe Keeper

The ADHD clothes-chair pile. Too clean to wash, too worn to put away.

ADHD laundry and folding. Why the clean pile never gets put away, and five ways to lower the bar.

## 5 free printable ADHD task cards (no email needed)
URL: https://neurotidy.co/free-adhd-task-cards/

These are five free printable ADHD task cards: one each for dishes, showers, doom piles, body doubling and bad days. Each card turns a task your brain refuses to start into three or four steps, and the last line of every card is the bad-day version, so there is always a size of the job you can actually do.

What these cards are

A task card is a small printed card that lives where the task happens. Dish card by the sink. Shower card on the bathroom mirror. Instead of holding "clean the kitchen" in your head as one giant blob, you read one line and do one line.

The five cards below are the free sample of the ADHD Home Reset, a 20-card deck built from more than 21,000 real ADHD threads about cleaning and home life. The full text of every free card is on this page, so you can read them before you print anything.

Download the free cards (PDF, no email needed)

Prefer the file itself? Open the PDF directly.

That link is a direct PDF. No signup, no checkout. Print it at home on A4 or letter paper and cut along the dashed lines.

Dish Rescue

Kitchen. Actually takes about 12 minutes.

Music or video ON before anything else.

Fill sink with hot soapy water. That's the whole commitment.

Drop dishes in. Walk away if you want. Soaking counts.

Still here? Wash until the song ends. Then decide again.

Bad day: rinse ONE mug for tomorrow's coffee. Done = win.

The 2-Alarm Shower

Bathroom. A full shower is 8 to 15 minutes, not an hour.

Set 2 alarms: total time, and 5-minutes-left.

Turn the water on BEFORE you decide anything.

Same wash order every time. Zero decisions inside.

At the final alarm: count slowly to 30, then step out at 30.

Bad day: wipes + dry shampoo + clean shirt = legitimate protocol.

Doom Pile Triage

Clutter. One pile takes about 10 minutes with 4 boxes.

Timer: 10 min. Music on. ONE pile.

Four boxes: Trash, Belongs elsewhere, Needs a decision, Keep here.

Sort mechanically. No verdicts today, just addresses.

Timer ends, you're allowed to stop. The decision box waits for a body double.

Bad day: remove exactly 3 objects. The monument cracks.

Body Double Call

Motivation. The most-reported game changer in the threads we read.

Text someone (ADHD friends get it instantly): "body double in 20 min?"

Phone on speaker. You both name your task out loud.

Work separately, together. Check in when one of you finishes.

Bad day: no friend free? Put on a cleaning video. Tornado mode is contagious.

The Bad-Day Floor

Recovery. Hitting the floor on a bad day = 10/10.

Body: teeth (wisps count), wipes + dry shampoo, one glass of water.

House: one mug rinsed, trash bag tied, outfit on the chair.

That is the WHOLE list. Everything else is officially cancelled today.

Bad day: this IS the bad-day card. You're already doing it right.

How to use the cards

Print the PDF and cut along the dashed lines. Plain paper works. Cardstock lasts longer.

Stick each card where the task happens. Dish Rescue by the sink, the 2-Alarm Shower on the bathroom mirror, Doom Pile Triage on the pile itself.

Read one line, do one line. Do not read ahead. The card is holding the list so your brain does not have to.

On a hard day, the bottom line of the card is the whole job. Doing that line counts as a full win, not a consolation prize.

Start with one card in one room. Add the next one only when the first feels boring.

If you want to know why this works better than willpower, the 5-minute reset and cleaning paralysis guides explain the mechanism. If you are not sure which card to start with, the 60-second mess-type quiz picks one for you.

What's next if these help

These five are a taste of the full deck. The ADHD Home Reset has all 20 cards (kitchen, laundry, bathroom, trash, doom piles, mornings and evenings) plus a short guide on why routines fail and what to use instead. It costs $9. Start with the free five though. If the free cards do not click, the deck will not either, and you will have lost nothing.


## The Out-of-Sight Out-of-Mind ADHD mess type
URL: https://neurotidy.co/adhd-mess-types/out-of-sight-out-of-mind/

The Out-of-Sight Out-of-Mind is the ADHD mess type where anything you cannot see stops existing, so everything stays out, and everything is everywhere. Closed drawers are where things go to die, and the fix is visible storage instead of hidden storage, not more discipline.

How to recognise it

The chair is covered, but on purpose, because if that stuff went into a drawer you would forget it exists. The counter holds everything you own, because the second something goes into a cupboard you forget you own it. Your daily-use items live in clear bins and open baskets, or they are gone forever. If it is not by the door in plain sight, it is a daily search party.

When you put everything away properly, you cannot find any of it for a week, so you pull it all back out. That is the Out-of-Sight Out-of-Mind, one of the four ADHD mess types.

What is actually going on

People call this ADHD object permanence. The phrase is colloquial, and the honest version is working memory: the mental list of what exists and what needs doing is shorter and drops items faster when they are out of view. You know the charger still exists in the drawer. Your brain just stopped listing it, so it stops being used and stops being put back.

So the mess is your brain's filing system doing its job. Things stay out because out is the only place they stay real. The object permanence guide and the cups everywhere guide walk through the mechanism, with the research it rests on. Clear bins and open baskets are not clutter. They are how your brain remembers the thing is even there.

The first card to use: Visible Systems

Clear bins, open baskets, and one launchpad by the door so leaving the house stops being a search party. Every daily-use item gets one visible home. Hooks beat drawers. Trays beat cupboards. The rest, the things you do not use every day, gets put away, so the visible layer stays small enough to read at a glance.

The card is built for a brain that needs to see it. It does not ask you to remember where things are. It makes remembering unnecessary.

This card is not in the free five. It lives in the $27 Whole Home Reset, which has the workspace and living-room visible-systems cards. Start with the free cards anyway. Doom Pile Triage and the Bad-Day Floor use the same format, and if the format works for you, the visible-systems cards will too.

Guides for the Out-of-Sight Out-of-Mind

ADHD object permanence and cleaning. What the term really means and how to build around it.

ADHD cups everywhere. A cup in every room is working memory, not slobbery.

Why is my room always messy? Designing the room for the brain you have.

Other types: the Doom Piler, the Floordrobe Keeper, the Churn and Burn. Not sure? Take the 60-second quiz.
